To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have identified a QTL on chromosome 1 that influences the response to E. maxuma H strain infection in a backcross between two inbred lines, and a QTL on chicken chromosome 1 that is associated with the response to Eimeria heterologous challenge; (2) the underlying pathways for the QTLs are related to immune response and cytokine signaling, with interleukin-2 and interleukin-12B being the most significant; and

the genetic architecture of resistance to E. maxima primary infection and protection to heterologous challenge in White Leghorn chickens are different, with the underlying pathways being immune response, and that IL-10 levels in serum are a phenotype of interest in the outcome of challenge.

(i) we have mapped the genetic architecture for resistance to primary E. maxima infection and protection against subsequent heterologous Eimeria challenge in the chicken; (ii) we have identified a QTL for IL-10 levels, a phenotype of interest for the outcome of challenge; and (iii) we have identified several candidate genes for the QTL, which are related to immune response, and in particular, IL-10 signaling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and dissection of the genetic architecture of resistance to E. maxima infection in the chicken.
the genetic control of E. maxima parasitism and the associated host immune response.

the identification of genomic regions that control host response to Eimeria infection, and the genes that underlie them, with the ultimate aim of identifying markers to be used in marker assisted selection for improved host resistance to coccidiosis.
